newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia trade surplus shows export recovery.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia trade surplus shows export recovery.

text.p: Malaysia's surprise 1.75 billion-ringgit ($700-million) trade surplus for March announced on Friday indicates a strong recovery in the country's exports after more than a year in the doldrums, most economists said.
They said the market for electronic products, which make up about 50 percent of the nation's exports, still remained easy because of a slump in the global electronics industry.
But strong export figures for other products, including petroleum products, plain plywood and pepper, had helped the trade balance.
The March data compares with a revised surplus of 368.5 million ringgit reported in February, and a surplus of 524 million in March 1996.
"This is a mind-boggling figure. This number is definitely positive (for the economy)," said Rajeev Malik, economist at Jardine Fleming International in Singapore.

"The market still expects Malaysia to register a small trade deficit for the year. But I think Malaysia will report a trade surplus for the year," said Daniel Lian, regional economist at Natwest Markets in Singapore.

"This means that there is a recovery in Malaysian exports," he said, adding it also showed that apart from being able to boost exports, Malaysia had also been able to keep a tight lid on imports of big-ticket items.
Malaysia's Statistics Department said exports in March grew by 2.8 percent to 18.68 billion ringgit year-on-year, while imports fell by 4.1 percent to 16.93 billion ringgit.
"We are definitely seeing an export recovery in Malaysia. This is the third month of consecutive export growth," said Seema Desai, economist at Schroders Securities in Singapore.
"We are already expecting a smaller current account deficit in 1997 compared to 1996," she said.

In 1996, Malaysia's trade deficit was 617.97 million ringgit against 9.36 billion ringgit in 1995. From January to March 1997, Malaysia posted a trade surplus of 2.016 billion ringgit, against a deficit of 1.357 billion in the same period of 1996.
Malaysia's central bank has forecast a current account deficit of 14.8 billion ringgit this year against 13 billion ringgit last year and 18.7 billion ringgit in 1995.
The Rating Agency Malaysia (RAM) on Friday said it expects a current account deficit of 15.69 billion ringgit in 1997.
"Underlying import growth in 1997 appears to be strong as we approach the deadline for the completion of a number of infrastructure projects in 1997 and 1998," RAM said.
Economists said the weakening of the yen and exports deferred from February due to the Moslem Eid al-Fitr and Chinese new year festivals, contributed to the positive data.
"In March alone the ringgit was up 16 percent (year-on-year) against the yen," said Malik. "But the trend will have to reverse, partly because the yen is moving the other way (now)."

"The (March) data tells us that there is a 38.1 percent increase in exports month-on-month. This increase is seasonal, because of festivals in February," said Jacqueline Ong, regional economist with research firm I.D.E.A. in Singapore.
"On the other hand, import figures show a 28.7 percent increase month-on-month, which is also a big jump. In February, imports showed a 22.2 percent decline," she said.
She said the situation may be different in April, when Malaysia had some large external payment commitments, including the purchase of a Boeing 777.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
